passages.happening:
Jesus is teaching by the lake again. The crowd is so large that he steps into a boat, sits down in it, and teaches from the water while the people stand along the shore.

He teaches in parables, short stories drawn from ordinary life. The first is about a farmer sowing seed. Some seed lands on the path, and birds eat it. Some lands on rocky ground, shoots up fast, and dries out in the sun because it has no root. Some falls among thorns, which grow up and choke it. And some lands on good soil and gives a crop of thirty, sixty, even a hundred times what was sown. Jesus ends with a call: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”
passages.hearers:
Most of the crowd knew farming from the inside. A farmer carried a bag of seed and threw it by hand in wide sweeps as he walked. Some seed always landed where it could not grow: on the hard path that ran across the field, on patches where rock lay just under a thin skin of earth, or among the roots of weeds.

Scholars still debate how a field was worked. Joachim Jeremias argued that in Jesus' land the seed was often sown first and ploughed in afterwards, which would explain seed on the path. K. D. White and others disagreed, and many now think farmers did it both ways. Either way, the waste in the story would have sounded normal.

What would not sound normal is the ending. A hundredfold was a sign of God's rich blessing. When Isaac had such a harvest, Genesis says, “he reaped a hundredfold. And the LORD blessed him” (Genesis 26:12). Three kinds of ground fail. Yet the harvest at the end is far bigger than the losses. The story is not about a bad year. It is about a harvest that wins in spite of everything.
passages.ot: The prophets often pictured God's word as seed. Through Isaiah God says that as rain makes the earth sprout and gives “seed to sow and food to eat,” so His word “will not return to Me empty” (Isaiah 55:10-11). Jeremiah warned the people, “do not sow among the thorns” (Jeremiah 4:3). Jesus' hearers knew that a story about sowing could be a story about God and his people.
passages.asks: The farmer does not stop sowing because some ground is poor. He throws the seed everywhere and trusts the harvest. Ask whether you have stopped speaking of God, or stopped listening to him, because so much seems wasted. And Jesus' closing words turn the story back on the listener: what kind of ground are you giving him today?

passages.happening: Later, when the crowd has gone, the Twelve and others who stayed near Jesus ask him about the parables. He tells them that “The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you,” but that to those outside everything comes in parables. Then he quotes words God once spoke to the prophet Isaiah, about people who look but do not see and listen but do not understand.
passages.hearers:
Two words need explaining. A parable (Greek parabolē) is something ‘set alongside’: a picture from daily life laid next to a truth about God. The Hebrew word behind it, mashal, covered proverbs, riddles, and stories such as the one Nathan told King David about a poor man's lamb (2 Samuel 12:1-7). A parable does not explain itself. It leaves the hearer to finish the thought.

In the Bible a ‘mystery’ is not a puzzle to be solved by clever people. It is a secret of God that he chooses to make known.

Who are the ‘outsiders’? Just before this, in 3:31-35, Jesus' own family stood ‘outside’ while the people sitting around him were called his mother and brothers. So the line between inside and outside is not about family or rank. It runs between those who come close and ask, and those who stay back. The disciples are no smarter than the crowd. In the very next verse Jesus asks why they do not understand. They are inside because they stayed and asked.
passages.ot:
The quotation comes from Isaiah 6, where God sends Isaiah to a nation that had already turned away. God warns him that his preaching will be met with closed ears: “Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving” (Isaiah 6:9).

There is one small difference. The Hebrew text of Isaiah ends with “turn and be healed” (Isaiah 6:10). Mark ends with “turn and be forgiven.” Mark's wording agrees with an Aramaic version of Isaiah called a Targum, which also speaks of forgiveness. Aramaic was the everyday language of Jesus' land, and some scholars see this as a sign that the saying comes from Jesus' own setting.
passages.hard:
Does Jesus tell parables so that people will not understand and will not be forgiven? On its plainest reading, verse 12 can sound that way, and readers have felt the difficulty from the start. Matthew, telling the same scene, puts it as a reason rather than a goal: people already see without seeing (Matthew 13:13).

Christians have answered in different ways. Some read the verse as God's judgment on people who had already refused him: the truth hidden in the story becomes a hardening for those who will not come near. Others, such as the scholar Joachim Jeremias, argued that the Aramaic behind the last line could mean ‘unless’: unless they turn and are forgiven. Many add that in Isaiah the words describe a people who had already hardened themselves.

The chapter itself gives two clues. Jesus spoke “to the extent that they could understand” (verse 33), and a lamp is meant to be put on a stand, not hidden (verse 21). Christians who stress God's choosing and those who stress human freedom have read this verse differently for centuries. Both agree on what the chapter keeps saying: listen.
passages.asks: The disciples did not understand either. The difference is that they stayed and asked. Ask whether you treat the hard parts of the Bible as a reason to walk away, or as a reason to come closer and ask Jesus what he means.

passages.happening:
Jesus explains the story. The seed is the word, God's message. The four kinds of ground are four ways of hearing it.

On the path, Satan takes the word away at once. On rocky ground, people receive it with joy but have no root, and they fall away when trouble comes. Among thorns, people hear it, but worries, the false promise of money, and the desire for other things choke it. On good soil, people hear the word, take it in, and bear a crop.
passages.hearers:
The second and third soils would have stung. Mark's first readers knew what “trouble or persecution comes because of the word” meant. Early tradition says Mark wrote in Rome in the years after Nero blamed Christians for the great fire of AD 64 and had many of them killed. Others place Mark in Syria or Galilee. Either way, his first readers had seen people turn back when following Jesus became costly.

The thorns were just as real. In a farming village a bad harvest could mean going hungry, and worry about bread and debt filled the day. Notice how the thorns work in the story. They do not kill the seed at once. They grow up beside it until there is no room left. Jesus calls wealth ‘deceitful’ because it promises a safety it cannot give.
passages.hard:
Did Jesus give this explanation, or did the early church add it? In the late 1800s the German scholar Adolf Jülicher argued that a true parable makes one point only. On that view a point-by-point explanation like this one looks like later church teaching, and many scholars followed him.

Others disagree. Craig Blomberg and others answer that ancient parables often made several points, one for each main character, and that teachers in Jesus' world sometimes explained their own stories. On that view the explanation fits Jesus well. Mark presents it as Jesus' own words, and that is how the church has read it.
passages.asks: These are not four kinds of people sorted forever. Most hearts hold some path, some rock, some thorns, and some good soil at the same time. Ask which one is crowding out God's word in you right now: a hard heart, a faith with no root, or a life too full to give it room.

passages.happening: Jesus asks a question with an obvious answer. Does anyone light a lamp and then hide it under a basket or a bed? No, it goes on a stand. What is hidden now will be brought into the light. Then he warns them to pay attention to what they hear, because the measure they use will be used for them, and even more will be given. Whoever has will receive more. Whoever does not have will lose even what he has.
passages.hearers:
A house lamp was a small clay dish of olive oil with a wick, and a village home might have only one. Hiding it would be silly. The ‘basket’ was a modios, a word Mark borrows from Latin, a grain measure that held about nine litres. Turned upside down, it would put a lamp out.

Mark's Greek says, word for word, ‘Does the lamp come?’ It is an odd way to speak of a lamp being brought in. Some readers think the choice of verb hints that Jesus himself is the lamp who has come. His light is hidden for now, inside riddles, but it is meant to shine.

The saying about measures came from the market. Grain was sold by the measure, and an honest or generous seller filled it full. Here the measure is how carefully a person listens.
passages.hard: “Whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.” This can sound unfair, as if the poor lose out. But Jesus is not speaking about money here. He is speaking about hearing. A person who takes in what he hears and acts on it understands more and more. A person who lets it slide past loses even the little he had grasped. Luke gives the same saying as “even what he thinks he has” (Luke 8:18).
passages.asks: Listening is not passive. Jesus says the way you listen decides how much you will receive. Ask what you do with what you hear from God: do you turn it over, act on it, and come back for more, or let it slide past?

passages.t: The seed that grows by itself
passages.happening: Jesus tells a parable found only in Mark. A man scatters seed. Then he goes to bed and gets up, night after night, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how. The earth produces the crop by itself: first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain. When the grain is ripe, he takes his sickle and reaps.
passages.hearers:
The key words are ‘All by itself’. Mark's Greek word is automatē, from which English gets ‘automatic’. The farmer does his part, the sowing and the reaping. But the growing is not his work. He cannot see it, cannot hurry it, and cannot explain it. He sleeps.

For a small group of disciples, following a teacher who had no army and no money, this mattered. God's kingdom would grow the way grain grows: quietly, out of sight, at its own pace, and surely.
passages.ot: The ending borrows the words of the prophet Joel: “Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe” (Joel 3:13). In Joel the harvest is the day when God judges the nations and puts things right. So the small seed and the patient waiting end in the great day of God.
passages.asks: Much of God's work happens while we are not watching. Ask where you are trying to force growth, in yourself, your family, or someone you pray for, that only God can give. Then ask what your part is: to sow, to wait, and to trust while you sleep.

passages.happening:
Jesus asks how to picture the kingdom of God. It is like a mustard seed, the smallest seed a farmer sows. Yet it grows into the largest plant in the garden, with branches big enough for birds to nest in its shade.

Mark then sums up. Jesus taught the crowds with many such parables, as much as they could take in. In private he explained everything to his disciples.
passages.hearers:
The plant was most likely black mustard, which grows wild in Galilee. Its seed is about a millimetre or two across, and in one season the plant can grow to two or three metres. The seed was so small that Jewish teachers used it as a byword for the tiniest amount.

Hearers would also catch a surprise. When the prophets pictured a great kingdom, they chose the cedar, the grandest tree they knew. Jesus chooses a garden plant. The kingdom will not arrive the way empires do. It begins as something people could easily overlook.
passages.ot: In Ezekiel, God plants a cedar on the mountains of Israel, and “Birds of every kind will nest under it” (Ezekiel 17:23). In Daniel a great tree stands for a mighty king, and “in its branches the birds of the air nested” (Daniel 4:12). Birds nesting in the branches was a picture of a kingdom that gives shelter to many peoples. Jesus takes that picture and attaches it to a mustard plant.
passages.hard: Is the mustard seed really ‘the smallest of all seeds’? Botanists know smaller ones, such as orchid seeds. But Jesus is speaking as a farmer would, of seeds “sown upon the earth” in a field or garden. Among those, mustard was the smallest anyone handled, and it was the common saying for something tiny. He is using the speech of the field, not a botany textbook.
passages.asks: God often starts small: a carpenter from Nazareth, twelve ordinary men, a few words dropped into a heart. Ask whether you have dismissed something because it looked too small to matter, in the church, in your home, or in your own faith.

passages.happening:
That evening Jesus says, “Let us cross to the other side.” The disciples take him across the lake in the boat he has been teaching from. A violent storm comes up. Waves break over the boat, and it starts to fill with water. Jesus is asleep at the back on a cushion. They wake him and cry, “Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?”

Jesus gets up, rebukes the wind, and tells the sea, “Silence!” “Be still!” The wind stops, and there is a great calm. He asks them why they are so afraid and whether they still have no faith. Now they are more frightened than before, and they ask each other, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?”
passages.hearers:
The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet below sea level, in a bowl ringed by hills. Cool air can pour down from the heights, especially from the east, and stir up sudden, violent storms. Several of these men were fishermen who had worked this lake all their lives. If they thought they were going to drown, the storm was real.

In 1986, during a drought, a fishing boat from about the time of Jesus was found in the mud of the lake shore. It is about eight metres long, big enough for a crew and some passengers. It helps us picture this scene: a small open boat, with Jesus at the back, the stern, where the man steering sat.

The words Mark uses matter. Jesus ‘rebukes’ the wind and tells the sea to ‘be silent’. These are the same two words he used on the unclean spirit in the synagogue (1:25). The storm is treated like a hostile power. Mark's Greek also repeats the word ‘great’: a great storm (verse 37), a great calm (verse 39), and great fear (verse 41). The disciples are more afraid after the calm than during the storm.
passages.ot:
For Israel the sea was a picture of chaos, and only God could rule it. The psalms say, “You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them” (Psalm 89:9), and of sailors in a storm, “He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29).

The story also echoes Jonah. There too a man sleeps in a boat during a great storm, frightened sailors wake him, they fear they will perish, the sea grows calm, and at the end “the men feared the LORD greatly” (Jonah 1:16). But Jonah was running from God, and the storm stopped only when he was thrown overboard. Jesus stops it with a word.

One psalm even cries to God, “Why are You sleeping?” (Psalm 44:23). The disciples pray much the same prayer to Jesus.
passages.hard: Why does Jesus scold them for lacking faith? They did turn to him for help, after all. But listen to what they said: “don’t You care that we are perishing?” Their fear was not only that the boat would sink. It was that Jesus did not care. Faith in Mark is trust in who Jesus is. They had seen him heal and cast out demons, and still they could not trust that he was for them. His question is not a sneer. It is an invitation to see.
passages.asks: The disciples obeyed Jesus, got into the boat, and still met a storm. Following him does not keep the storms away. Ask whether, in your hardest moments, you have doubted not only God's power but his care. Then sit with their question, the one Mark leaves open: who is this?
